subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: During ventricular systole, the atrioventricular valves close because:
options: Atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure
The ventricles are relaxing and filling
Ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure
The semilunar valves are open
questions.explain: As the ventricles contract their pressure rises above that of the atria, forcing the AV valves shut to prevent backflow.

questions.q: When a fully turgid plant cell has its pressure potential exactly balancing its solute potential, its water potential is zero, meaning:
options: water rushes in rapidly
there is no net movement of water into or out of the cell when surrounded by pure water
the cell wall has burst
the cell is plasmolysed
questions.explain: At full turgor the inward pressure potential equals the solute potential in magnitude, giving Psi = 0, so no net water movement occurs with pure water outside.

questions.q: As an organism increases in size, why does it require a specialised exchange surface?
options: Volume increases more slowly than surface area
Its surface-area-to-volume ratio increases, slowing diffusion
Its surface-area-to-volume ratio decreases, so diffusion across the body surface cannot meet metabolic demand
Larger cells respire anaerobically and need no oxygen
questions.explain: As size increases, volume rises faster than surface area, so the SA:V ratio falls and the body surface alone cannot supply the cells.

questions.q: A plant cell becomes plasmolysed when placed in a concentrated salt solution because:
options: water enters the cell, pushing the membrane against the wall
water leaves the cell by osmosis, so the protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall
salt is actively pumped out of the cell
the cell wall ruptures
questions.explain: The external solution has a lower (more negative) water potential, so water leaves the cell and the plasma membrane pulls away from the wall.

questions.q: The sino-atrial node (SAN) is described as the pacemaker of the heart because it:
options: Prevents the atria and ventricles from contracting together
Receives blood from the vena cava
Initiates waves of excitation that set the basic heart rate
Conducts the impulse to the ventricles after a delay
questions.explain: The SAN spontaneously generates waves of depolarisation that spread across the atria and set the heart's intrinsic rhythm.

questions.q: The enzyme RuBisCO can also catalyse a reaction between RuBP and oxygen. What is the effect of this when CO2 levels are very low?
options: It speeds up photolysis
It increases the rate of glucose synthesis
It reduces the efficiency of carbon fixation
It produces extra ATP
questions.explain: When CO2 is scarce, RuBisCO fixes oxygen instead, wastefully reducing the efficiency of the Calvin cycle.

questions.q: In which direction are protons pumped to create the gradient that drives ATP synthesis in the chloroplast?
options: From the stroma into the thylakoid space
Out of the chloroplast entirely
From the cytoplasm into the stroma
From the thylakoid space into the stroma
questions.explain: Protons are moved into the thylakoid space, and their return to the stroma through ATP synthase generates ATP.

questions.q: A potometer measures the rate of water uptake by a shoot, which is used as an estimate of transpiration. A key assumption is that:
options: Stomata are fully closed throughout
Water uptake exactly equals water lost as vapour
No water is used in photosynthesis or stored in cells
The shoot continues to grow during the experiment
questions.explain: The potometer assumes that virtually all water taken up is lost in transpiration, though a small amount is actually used by the plant.

questions.q: A flatworm relies on diffusion across its body surface for gas exchange. Which feature of its body makes this possible despite having no specialised system?
options: A flattened shape giving a large surface area and short diffusion distance to all cells
A closed circulatory system carrying haemoglobin
A thick, impermeable cuticle
A high metabolic rate requiring rapid oxygen delivery
questions.explain: Its flat, thin body provides a large SA:V ratio and ensures no cell is far from the surface, so diffusion alone suffices.

questions.q: Companion cells are essential to phloem transport because they:
options: Conduct water under tension like xylem vessels
Store starch for the sieve tubes
Provide ATP and actively load sucrose into the sieve tube elements
Contain no organelles, reducing resistance to flow
questions.explain: Companion cells, rich in mitochondria, actively load sucrose into sieve tubes at the source, driving mass flow.

questions.q: In the co-transport of glucose in the ileum, glucose is absorbed into the epithelial cell because:
options: glucose is actively pumped out of the cell
a sodium-glucose co-transporter carries glucose in alongside Na+ moving down its gradient
glucose is pumped directly by ATP into the cell
glucose diffuses freely through the phospholipid bilayer
questions.explain: Na+ entering down its gradient (maintained by the Na+/K+ pump) drives glucose into the cell against its gradient via the co-transporter.

questions.q: Cells specialised for absorption, such as the epithelial cells of the ileum, increase their rate of uptake by having:
options: no mitochondria
a thicker cell wall
fewer carrier proteins to reduce competition
microvilli that greatly increase the surface area of the membrane for transport proteins
questions.explain: Microvilli increase the membrane surface area, providing more sites for carrier and co-transport proteins and so faster absorption.

questions.q: Tissue fluid is formed at the arteriole end of a capillary mainly because:
options: The low water potential of the blood draws water out
Hydrostatic (blood) pressure exceeds the oncotic pull of plasma proteins, forcing fluid out
Oncotic pressure exceeds hydrostatic pressure
Plasma proteins leave the capillary
questions.explain: At the arteriole end high hydrostatic pressure outweighs the water potential gradient created by plasma proteins, so fluid is forced out.

questions.q: Most tissue fluid is returned to the circulation by the:
options: Active transport across the capillary wall
Combination of osmotic return at the venule end and drainage by the lymphatic system
Venule end of the capillary only, driven by osmosis
Arteriole end of the capillary
questions.explain: Some fluid re-enters at the venule end down a water-potential gradient, and the excess is collected and returned by the lymphatic system.

questions.q: In the Calvin cycle, what is the role of ATP and reduced NADP in converting GP to triose phosphate (TP)?
options: They regenerate RuBP directly from CO2
ATP oxidises GP while NADP fixes carbon
They catalyse photolysis of water
ATP provides energy and reduced NADP provides hydrogen to reduce GP to TP
questions.explain: GP is reduced to triose phosphate using energy from ATP and hydrogen from reduced NADP.

questions.q: Two limiting-factor curves are plotted at different CO2 concentrations against light intensity. The higher CO2 curve plateaus at a greater rate. What does this show?
options: CO2 was limiting the rate where the lower curve plateaued
Photosynthesis is independent of CO2
Temperature is the only limiting factor
Light is never limiting
questions.explain: A higher plateau at greater CO2 shows that CO2 had been limiting the rate of the lower-concentration curve.

questions.q: The myoglobin dissociation curve lies to the LEFT of the haemoglobin curve, which means myoglobin:
options: Releases oxygen at higher partial pressures than haemoglobin
Carries four oxygen molecules like haemoglobin
Has a higher affinity for oxygen and acts as an oxygen store in muscle
Cannot bind oxygen at low partial pressures
questions.explain: Myoglobin's high oxygen affinity means it only releases oxygen at very low partial pressures, acting as a reserve store in muscle.

questions.q: What are the products of the photolysis of water during the light-dependent stage?
options: Carbon dioxide, protons and ATP
ATP, reduced NADP and CO2
Electrons, protons and oxygen
Glucose, oxygen and water
questions.explain: Splitting water yields electrons for photosystem II, protons for the gradient, and oxygen as a by-product.

questions.q: Which factor would increase the permeability of a cell membrane?
options: An increase in temperature, increasing phospholipid movement and creating gaps
Increasing cholesterol content
Removal of all membrane proteins
A decrease in temperature, increasing phospholipid order
questions.explain: Higher temperatures increase phospholipid kinetic energy and fluidity, and can denature membrane proteins, increasing permeability.

questions.q: Why can small non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the membrane by simple diffusion?
options: They are repelled by the hydrophobic core
They require carrier proteins
They are actively transported
They are small and non-polar, so they dissolve in and pass through the hydrophobic phospholipid bilayer
questions.explain: Being small and non-polar, these molecules dissolve in the lipid bilayer and diffuse directly across down their gradient.

questions.q: Cholesterol contributes to membrane stability at low temperatures by:
options: forming hydrophilic channels
preventing the phospholipids from packing too closely, so the membrane does not become too rigid and stays fluid
allowing phospholipids to pack tightly and freeze solid
increasing active transport
questions.explain: At low temperatures cholesterol stops phospholipids packing tightly together, maintaining fluidity and preventing the membrane becoming too rigid.

questions.q: What overall role does the chloroplast envelope (double membrane) play?
options: It contains the photosystems
It is the site of the Calvin cycle
It controls the entry and exit of substances such as CO2 and sugars
It splits water during photolysis
questions.explain: The chloroplast envelope regulates exchange of materials, including the movement of CO2 in and products out.

questions.q: During inspiration in a mammal, the pressure in the thorax falls because:
options: The diaphragm relaxes and domes upward
The volume of the thoracic cavity increases as the diaphragm flattens and the ribs move up and out
The external intercostal muscles relax
Surfactant reduces the surface tension of the alveoli
questions.explain: Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostals increases thoracic volume, lowering pressure below atmospheric so air flows in.

questions.q: Spongy mesophyll in a leaf is adapted for gas exchange because:
options: It transports water to the stomata
Air spaces between loosely packed cells provide a large moist surface for diffusion
It actively pumps carbon dioxide into the cells
It contains many chloroplasts for trapping light
questions.explain: Loosely packed cells with interconnected air spaces give a large moist surface area, allowing gases to diffuse to and from photosynthesising cells.

questions.q: In the human gas-exchange system, which sequence correctly lists the path of air during inspiration?
options: Trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli
Bronchioles, bronchi, trachea, alveoli
Bronchi, trachea, bronchioles, alveoli
Trachea, bronchioles, bronchi, alveoli
questions.explain: Air passes from the trachea to the bronchi, then the finer bronchioles, and finally reaches the alveoli where exchange occurs.

questions.q: Beetroot pieces leak red pigment more rapidly when placed in 50% ethanol than in water because ethanol:
options: denatures the pigment so it appears redder
lowers the temperature of the cells
dissolves and disrupts the phospholipid bilayer, increasing membrane permeability
increases the pressure potential of the cells
questions.explain: Organic solvents such as ethanol dissolve membrane lipids and disrupt the bilayer, increasing permeability so the pigment leaks out faster.

questions.q: A plant cell with a water potential of -500 kPa is placed in a solution of water potential -300 kPa. The cell will:
options: lose water and become flaccid
plasmolyse rapidly
show no net water movement
gain water by osmosis because the solution has a higher (less negative) water potential
questions.explain: Water moves from higher to lower water potential, so water enters the cell (from -300 to -500), and the cell gains water and becomes more turgid.

questions.q: What is the function of reduced NADP produced in the light-dependent reactions?
options: It carries hydrogen to reduce GP to triose phosphate in the Calvin cycle
It splits water during photolysis
It is the final electron acceptor
It pumps protons across the thylakoid membrane
questions.explain: Reduced NADP supplies the hydrogen needed to reduce GP to triose phosphate in the stroma.

questions.q: In a commercial greenhouse, why might a grower add a carbon dioxide generator alongside extra lighting?
options: To denature plant enzymes
To stop the Calvin cycle
To prevent CO2 from becoming the limiting factor when light is plentiful
To reduce the rate of photosynthesis
questions.explain: With abundant light, raising CO2 stops it from limiting photosynthesis, allowing a higher overall rate.

questions.q: The fluid-mosaic model describes the cell membrane as:
options: a single layer of phospholipids
a continuous protein sheet with no lipid
a rigid layer of protein sandwiched between lipid
a fluid phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in a mosaic pattern
questions.explain: The model depicts a fluid bilayer in which proteins are scattered like a mosaic and can move laterally within the membrane.
